title: Ὀρνιθοθήρας καὶ ἄγριαι καὶ ἥμεραι περιστεραί
titleEn: The Fowler and the Wild and Tame Doves
part: The Fowler and the Wild and Tame Doves (Chambry 282 · Perry 238)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 282 (= Perry 238). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ὀρνιθοθήρας πετάσας τὰ λίνα ἐκ τῶν ἡμέρων περιστερῶν προσέδησεν· εἶτα ἀποστὰς αὐτὸς πόρρωθεν ἀπεκαραδόκει τὸ μέλλον.
sentences.tr: Ornithothēras petasas ta lina ek tōn hēmerōn peristerōn prosedēsen· eita apostas autos porrōthen apekaradokei to mellon.
sentences.l: A fowler, having spread out his nets, made them fast from his tame doves; then, having withdrawn, he himself watched from a distance for what was to come.
sentences.i: A fowler spread out his nets and made them fast to his tame doves; then he drew off and watched from a distance to see what would happen.
sentences.n: Tame doves were kept as decoys and tethered where the nets were set, so that wild birds coming down to them fell into the trap: the whole fable turns on that arrangement. ἐκ … προσέδησεν — the nets are made fast from the doves, that is, rigged to the tethered decoys themselves. ἀποκαραδοκέω is to crane the head forward and watch intently for something — it returns at fable 284, again of a fowler at his nets. τὸ μέλλον, the participle under the article, is simply 'the thing about to be'.

sentences.t: Ἀγρίων δὲ ταύταις προσελθουσῶν καὶ τοῖς βρόχοις ἐμπλακεισῶν, προσδραμὼν συλλαμβάνειν αὐτὰς ἐπειρᾶτο.
sentences.tr: Agriōn de tautais proselthousōn kai tois brochois emplakeisōn, prosdramōn syllambanein autas epeirato.
sentences.l: And when wild ones had come to these and had been entangled in the nooses, he ran up and tried to seize them.
sentences.n: A genitive absolute — Ἀγρίων … προσελθουσῶν … ἐμπλακεισῶν — the standard way of setting the circumstances before the main clause; the feminine endings alone tell us that the wild ones are doves. ἐμπλακεισῶν is the aorist passive participle of ἐμπλέκω, 'be tangled up in'.

sentences.t: Τῶν δὲ αἰτιωμένων τὰς ἡμέρους, εἴγε ὁμόφυλοι οὖσαι αὐταῖς τὸν δόλον οὐ προεμήνυσαν, ἐκεῖναι ὑποτυχοῦσαι ἔφασαν· « Ἀλλ’ ἡμῖν γε ἄμεινον δεσπότας φυλάττεσθαι ἢ τῇ ἡμετέρᾳ συγγενείᾳ χαρίζεσθαι. »
sentences.tr: Tōn de aitiōmenōn tas hēmerous, eige homophyloi ousai autais ton dolon ou proemēnysan, ekeinai hypotychousai ephasan· « All’ hēmin ge ameinon despotas phylattesthai ē tēi hēmeterāi syngeneiāi charizesthai. »
sentences.l: And when these blamed the tame ones, in that, being of the same stock as them, they had not disclosed the trick beforehand, those, taking-up-the-word, said: « But for us at any rate it is better to guard against our masters than to do a kindness to our own kin. »
sentences.i: And when they blamed the tame doves for not warning their own kind of the trick beforehand, the tame ones answered: « For us, at least, it is better to be on our guard against our masters than to oblige our own kin. »
sentences.n: εἴγε introduces the ground of the charge, 'seeing that, in that' — it gives the accusers' reason, not the narrator's. ὁμόφυλος takes a dative of the kin it is kin to, so αὐταῖς belongs with ὁμόφυλοι οὖσαι, 'being of the same stock as them', and προεμήνυσαν stands without an expressed indirect object. ὑποτυχοῦσαι is the regular fable word for cutting in with an answer; the house rendering is 'taking-up-the-word'. φυλάττομαι in the middle takes a plain accusative of the party one is on guard against.

sentences.t: Οὕτω καὶ τῶν οἰκετῶν οὐ μεμπτέοι εἰσὶν ὅσοι δι’ ἀγάπην τῶν οἰκείων δεσποτῶν παραπίπτουσι τῆς τῶν οἰκείων συγγενῶν φιλίας.
sentences.tr: Houtō kai tōn oiketōn ou mempteoi eisin hosoi di’ agapēn tōn oikeiōn despotōn parapiptousi tēs tōn oikeiōn syngenōn philias.
sentences.l: So too, among household slaves, those are not to be blamed who, through love of their own masters, fall away from the friendship of their own kinsmen.
sentences.n: μεμπτέος is a verbal adjective in -τέος, which carries the sense of what must or should be done: 'to be blamed'. παραπίπτω with the genitive is to miss a thing, to let it slip past. The same closing shape — 'So too, among X, those are not to be blamed who…' — stands at fable 175.
